paragraphs: Sequence-to-sequence learning turns an input such as a sentence into an output whose length can differ. Recurrent networks traditionally perform this job, but their sequential computations make it difficult to use parallel hardware fully. This paper asks whether convolutions can provide a faster and more effective alternative for the entire model.

The proposed architecture uses convolutional networks throughout. Gated linear units help gradients propagate, while a separate attention module in every decoder layer lets the output computation consult the input. During training, computations across sequence elements can run in parallel. The number of nonlinear transformations also stays independent of sequence length, which the authors identify as an optimization advantage.

On WMT’14 English–German and English–French translation, the model exceeds the accuracy of the deep LSTM setup of Wu et al. while reporting an order-of-magnitude speed advantage on both CPU and GPU. These translation results establish that recurrence is not necessary for strong sequence modeling in the evaluated setting.
icml-2017-convolutional-sequence-to-sequ.tldr: A fully convolutional sequence model improves translation accuracy and speed over the compared recurrent model.

paragraphs: Choosing initial centers matters for k-means clustering. k-Means++ has a useful expected approximation guarantee, but selecting its centers requires k sequential passes over the data. That dependence makes initialization expensive on very large datasets. The distributed alternative, k-Means||, reduces sequential rounds, raising the question of how much solution quality those savings cost.

The paper analyzes k-Means|| as a function of its two practical tuning choices: the number of rounds and the oversampling factor. The resulting bound covers any number of rounds and oversampling factors greater than k. It therefore connects implementation choices directly to an expected quality guarantee rather than treating the number of rounds as fixed by a single prescription.

The analysis shows that even a small constant number of rounds can produce provably good clusterings, helping explain the algorithm’s practical success. A constructed hard instance also shows why an additive error term cannot generally disappear when fewer than k−1 rounds are used. The contribution combines a positive scalability guarantee with a matching structural limitation.
icml-2017-distributed-and-provably-good-.tldr: A parameter-sensitive analysis explains why distributed k-means initialization works well with only a few rounds.

paragraphs: Quantile regression models features of a response distribution such as its median rather than only its mean. Estimating a linear quantile model becomes difficult when the number of predictors greatly exceeds the number of observations. This paper studies how structural knowledge about the unknown coefficients can make that high-dimensional estimation problem manageable.

The authors assume that the true parameter has a small value under an atomic norm, a mathematical way of representing low-complexity structure. They incorporate that norm as a regularizer in the quantile regression estimator. The analysis then connects recovery behavior to the geometry of the assumed structure and to statistical properties of the estimation problem.

The paper gives sample-complexity conditions for consistent recovery and finite-sample bounds on estimation error. Synthetic experiments support the theoretical conclusions. Its main contribution is an account of which structural and statistical features govern estimation accuracy; the reported evidence does not establish performance on a particular real-world application.
icml-2017-high-dimensional-structured-qu.tldr: Atomic-norm regularization gives structured high-dimensional quantile regression explicit sample and error guarantees.

paragraphs: In nonconvex optimization, a small gradient can indicate either a useful minimum or a saddle point. Ordinary first-order convergence guarantees do not distinguish these outcomes. This paper studies whether a small modification to gradient descent can reach second-order stationary points without paying a large cost for the dimension of the parameter space.

The method perturbs gradient descent, and its analysis uses a new characterization of the geometry near saddle points. The authors show convergence to second-order stationarity with only polylogarithmic dependence on dimension. Up to logarithmic factors, the iteration rate matches the familiar rate for gradient descent to reach first-order stationarity.

When all saddle points are non-degenerate, the second-order stationary points are local minima, giving the result a direct optimization interpretation. The paper also applies the theory to obtain sharp global convergence rates for matrix factorization. The distinction matters: reaching a local minimum follows under the stated saddle-point condition, while global convergence is demonstrated for the particular matrix-factorization application.
icml-2017-how-to-escape-saddle-points-ef.tldr: Perturbed gradient descent escapes saddles with only a small additional iteration cost under the analyzed conditions.

paragraphs: Different experts can organize the same dataset in legitimately different ways. Methods that merge all expert input into one clustering may therefore erase useful alternative views, especially when no ground truth is available. This paper treats disagreement as a possible sign of multiple clustering structures while also accounting for uncertainty in individual experts.

The authors introduce a Bayesian model that jointly learns expert views, the clustering associated with each view, and expert confidence. Variational inference estimates these coupled quantities. Experts with higher inferred confidence receive more influence within a view, allowing the model to distinguish unreliable input from meaningful differences in how the data should be grouped.

Experiments cover synthetic data, benchmark datasets, and a disease-subtyping application. The approach outperforms the compared meta-clustering, semi-supervised, semi-crowdsourced, and consensus-clustering baselines. The reported contribution is thus both representational and practical: it discovers multiple organizations of the data while improving clustering quality within those views, rather than requiring all experts to agree on one answer.
icml-2017-multiple-clustering-views-from.tldr: A Bayesian model separates expert disagreement into multiple clustering views while learning how much to trust each expert.

paragraphs: Deep-network training is nonconvex, yet optimization often succeeds without getting trapped at visibly poor solutions. One proposed explanation is that local minima are already close to globally optimal. This paper investigates that explanation mathematically for a particular family of sufficiently wide, fully connected neural networks.

The setting uses squared loss and an analytic activation function. At least one hidden layer must contain more units than there are training examples, and the network must have a pyramidal structure from that layer onward. These architectural and functional assumptions are central to the result: they specify the class of loss surfaces being characterized.

Under those conditions, the authors show that almost all local minima are globally optimal. This strengthens the suggestion that good training behavior can arise from favorable loss-surface geometry. It is a statement about the quality of local minima in the analyzed model class; it does not by itself give a convergence rate for a training algorithm or establish the same geometry for every neural architecture.
icml-2017-the-loss-surface-of-deep-and-w.tldr: For a specified wide network class, almost all local minima of the training loss are globally optimal.

paragraphs: A knowledge base can be represented as a three-way binary tensor whose entries describe whether relational facts hold. Canonical Tensor Decomposition, or CP, is a natural model for completing missing entries, yet existing implementations had performed poorly against competing knowledge-base completion methods. This paper examines whether the problem lies in CP itself or in how it is trained and formulated.

The authors propose a regularizer based on tensor nuclear p-norms. They also reformulate the completion problem so that results are invariant to arbitrary choices about including a predicate or its reciprocal in the dataset. These changes address both the preference imposed on learned factors and the representation of relational direction.

Together, the two changes allow CP to surpass the then-current state of the art on several datasets. Applying the same ideas to ComplEx produces further improvements. The findings suggest that regularization and dataset formulation can materially change the apparent capabilities of a tensor model, although the abstract does not separate the numerical contribution of each modification.
icml-2018-canonical-tensor-decomposition.tldr: Better regularization and reciprocal-relation handling make CP competitive for knowledge-base completion and also improve ComplEx.

paragraphs: Learning a causal graph often combines passive observations with experiments that intervene on selected variables. Prior identifiability results considered perfect interventions, which remove the dependence of a targeted variable on its direct causes. Many interventions, including biological manipulations, instead alter those dependencies without completely removing them.

This paper extends the theory to such general interventions. It defines and characterizes the interventional Markov equivalence class: the set of causal directed acyclic graphs that remain indistinguishable given the available experimental information. The characterization explains what causal structure can be identified when an intervention changes a mechanism but does not necessarily sever its incoming relationships.

The authors also propose a provably consistent algorithm for learning graphs in this setting and evaluate it on simulated and biological datasets. The contribution connects a broader experimental model to both an identifiability theory and a learning procedure. Its guarantee concerns recovery within the stated intervention setting; the abstract does not claim that every intervention design uniquely identifies a single causal graph.
icml-2018-characterizing-and-learning-eq.tldr: The paper characterizes what general interventions reveal about causal graphs and gives a consistent learning algorithm.

paragraphs: Distributed gradient computation can be slowed both by workers that finish late and by the amount of information workers must send. Adding redundant computation can tolerate slow workers, but redundancy also has a cost. This paper studies those competing demands together rather than optimizing straggler tolerance alone.

The authors characterize a fundamental tradeoff among computation load, straggler tolerance, and communication cost. They construct a coding scheme that achieves the optimal tradeoff using recursive polynomials. The scheme codes across both data subsets and gradient-vector components, giving it control over the amount of work assigned and the amount of information communicated.

Implementations on Amazon EC2 use Python and mpi4py. The reported experiments preserve generalization error while reducing running time by 32% relative to uncoded schemes and 23% relative to a prior straggler-focused coded method. These results support the practical value of jointly managing communication and redundant computation for the distributed learning workloads evaluated.
icml-2018-communication-computation-effi.tldr: Gradient coding jointly optimizes computation, communication, and straggler tolerance to reduce distributed training time.

paragraphs: Convolutional sparse coding represents long signals using patterns that can recur at different positions. Solving the associated optimization problem efficiently is important when signals are large enough to benefit from multiple processors. This paper introduces DICOD, a distributed coordinate-descent algorithm designed around the local structure of that computation.

DICOD uses local message passing, reducing the need for broad communication between workers. Its updates are locally greedy: workers make useful coordinate choices within their own regions. The authors argue that this choice can accelerate optimization compared with a globally greedy coordinate-selection strategy, so parallelism changes more than simply how many updates happen at once.

The paper proves convergence and highlights a speedup that can be super-linear in the number of cores. Empirical comparisons with existing methods support its acceleration properties. The contribution is specifically an efficient solver for convolutional sparse coding; the abstract does not attribute the gains to a new signal representation or report an improvement in downstream predictive accuracy.
icml-2018-dicod-distributed-convolutiona.tldr: DICOD uses local, distributed coordinate updates to accelerate convolutional sparse coding with a convergence guarantee.

paragraphs: Fast implementations of neural-network convolutions often allocate extra memory to reorganize data or support the chosen computation algorithm. On a memory-constrained device, that temporary storage can reduce the network size that fits. The paper also argues that relying on general high-performance routines can leave convolution-specific performance opportunities unused.

The authors develop a carefully implemented direct convolution approach. Its aim is to compute convolution without the additional memory overhead used by the compared high-performance routines. The relevant distinction is temporary overhead from the implementation, rather than eliminating the memory required to hold a model, its inputs, or its outputs.

Across conventional and embedded CPU architectures, the abstract reports performance improvements ranging from 10% to 400% over existing implementations. It also reports better scaling as the number of threads increases, with less performance degradation. The results make direct convolution a practical systems alternative in the tested CPU settings, particularly where spare memory is limited; they do not establish the same performance comparison for GPUs.
icml-2018-high-performance-zero-memory-o.tldr: Carefully implemented direct CPU convolutions reduce temporary memory overhead while improving speed and thread scaling.

paragraphs: Deep networks can fit training data exactly and still generalize well, a combination often treated as distinctive to deep learning. This paper shows that classical kernel methods exhibit similar behavior. That comparison provides a simpler setting in which to examine why interpolation need not destroy test performance.

Experiments on six real-world and two synthetic datasets find strong test performance from kernel machines with zero classification error or nearly zero regression error. The theory gives a lower bound showing that norms of zero-loss solutions for smooth kernels grow nearly exponentially with data size, making existing norm-based bounds uninformative for these interpolating solutions.

Additional experiments show that Laplacian kernels readily fit random labels, whereas smooth Gaussian kernels require many more epochs on noisy data. Their similar test performance leads the authors to suggest that generalization depends more on kernel properties than on optimization in these comparisons. The paper calls for better theory of interpolating kernel methods as part of understanding corresponding phenomena in deep networks.
icml-2018-to-understand-deep-learning-we.tldr: Interpolating kernel methods reproduce important deep-learning generalization phenomena that existing bounds fail to explain.

paragraphs: In repeated posted-price auctions, a seller learns how to price a good while a buyer may strategically accept or reject offers. The buyer in this paper has a fixed private valuation and optimizes discounted surplus across interactions. This makes the learning problem different from estimating willingness to pay from an immediately truthful response.

The authors introduce a pricing algorithm whose offered prices never decrease. Its strategic regret has a tight Θ(log log T) bound, where T is the number of rounds. The method is horizon-independent, so its operation does not require knowing the eventual interaction length in advance, and it satisfies the paper’s weak-consistency requirement.

This establishes the existence of a no-regret pricing strategy with those properties, resolving the stated open question. The paper also shows that nondecreasing prices are nearly necessary for weakly consistent no-regret algorithms. Both conclusions belong to the specific repeated-auction model with one strategic buyer and a fixed valuation, rather than a general market with changing or competing buyers.
icml-2018-weakly-consistent-optimal-pric.tldr: A nondecreasing-price strategy achieves tight doubly logarithmic strategic regret without knowing the auction horizon.

paragraphs: AdaGrad adjusts optimization steps using gradients accumulated during training, reducing the need to hand-design a learning-rate schedule. Although widely used in large-scale learning, its established guarantees had focused on convex or online optimization. This paper analyzes the norm-based variant, AdaGrad-Norm, on smooth nonconvex objectives.

The authors prove convergence to stationary points in both stochastic and deterministic settings. In the stochastic case, the stated rate is O(log(N)/√N); in the batch setting it is the optimal O(1/N) rate under their analysis. These results describe how the method behaves when the objective can contain multiple minima and saddles, rather than assuming convexity.

Theoretical findings and extensive numerical experiments also indicate robustness to an unknown Lipschitz constant and unknown gradient-noise level. That robustness helps explain the appeal of adapting steps from observed gradients. The endpoint guaranteed here is stationarity, which should not be read as a universal guarantee of reaching the global optimum of a nonconvex problem.
icml-2019-adagrad-stepsizes-sharp-conver.tldr: AdaGrad-Norm receives sharp nonconvex stationarity guarantees and evidence of robustness to unknown smoothness and noise.

paragraphs: A generative model can learn the dominant variation in medical waveforms while overlooking subtle features that matter for prediction. For example, a signal associated with a clinical outcome may explain little of the overall variation in electrocardiograms. This paper aims to preserve that predictive information in a latent representation that can also support interpretation.

The proposed training objective uses a black-box discriminative model as a regularizer for a generative latent-variable model. This encourages the representation to retain variations relevant to the predictor, rather than focusing exclusively on reconstructing common patterns. The resulting model lets researchers visualize and measure changes in the data that influence the black-box prediction.

The authors study electrocardiogram-based prediction of clinically interesting outcomes. Evaluation includes synthetic and real data, statistical summaries, and an experiment involving a physician. The contribution is a way to inspect predictive variation through a generative representation; the abstract does not establish that the resulting explanations identify causal mechanisms or improve patient outcomes.
icml-2019-discriminative-regularization-.tldr: Discriminative regularization helps generative representations retain and visualize subtle features that influence clinical predictions.

paragraphs: First-order optimization methods can avoid saddles in many unconstrained problems, but those results do not automatically handle constraints or critical points on a boundary. This paper studies nonconcave maximization over a product of simplices, a domain that appears when variables represent distributions or normalized allocations.

The authors analyze a variant of Multiplicative Weights Update for a twice continuously differentiable objective. Their proof combines dynamical-systems techniques with a connection between the Baum–Eagon inequality and multiplicative updates. This allows the analysis to address the geometry of the constrained feasible set instead of requiring all relevant critical points to lie in its interior.

For sufficiently small step sizes, the method converges almost always to critical points satisfying second-order Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions. The result strengthens the theoretical understanding of a familiar distributed optimization procedure. Second-order KKT conditions are the relevant constrained optimality criterion here; the abstract does not claim that all such points are global maximizers of the nonconcave objective.
icml-2019-multiplicative-weights-updates.tldr: Multiplicative weights almost always reaches second-order constrained stationary points for the analyzed nonconcave problems.

paragraphs: Neural networks can represent extremely complicated functions, including arbitrary labels on training examples. Expressive capacity alone, however, does not determine which patterns a network learns first. This paper studies that distinction through the frequencies of the functions learned during training.

Using Fourier analysis, the authors identify a bias toward low-frequency functions: patterns that vary broadly across the input rather than fluctuating rapidly in small regions. The bias appears as a frequency-dependent learning speed. This offers a way to understand why an overparameterized network can prioritize comparatively simple, broadly shared patterns despite having enough capacity to memorize more complicated ones.

The paper also examines the geometry of the data manifold. Its theoretical and empirical evidence indicates that higher-frequency functions can become easier to learn as manifold complexity increases. Thus the learning preference is not described solely by the network’s expressive power; it also depends on how the data occupy the input space. The abstract presents this as an explanatory property, rather than a universal generalization guarantee.
icml-2019-on-the-spectral-bias-of-neural.tldr: Networks learn lower frequencies preferentially, while the geometry of the data manifold changes how difficult higher frequencies are.

paragraphs: Extreme multi-label learning must predict relevant labels from a very large label set. Sparse local embeddings, exemplified by SLEEC, had shown strong practical promise, but their statistical convergence and oracle behavior were not well understood. This paper builds a theoretical framework for a related estimator with nonconvex regularization.

The proposed framework combines the SLEEC setting with a nonconvex penalty. The authors prove an oracle property, meaning that the estimator can perform as well as if the underlying model were known beforehand in the formal setting analyzed. They also establish a statistical convergence rate and show that an additional condition on the sizes of underlying model entries yields an improved rate.

Extensive numerical experiments support the theory and show advantages over the compared estimators. The work therefore adds statistical justification to a successful approach for large label spaces while proposing an estimator with favorable measured behavior. The oracle statement is a conditional theoretical property, not a claim that the algorithm is given the true model during training.
icml-2019-sparse-extreme-multi-label-lea.tldr: A nonconvex sparse-embedding estimator for extreme multi-label learning gains oracle and convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Training on synthetic images can reduce data-collection costs, but the resulting model may perform poorly on real images. ImageNet initialization often helps, yet retaining its useful knowledge typically depends on manually tuned stopping rules and learning rates. This paper makes preservation of the pretrained representation an explicit part of synthetic-data training.

The framework encourages the evolving model to maintain representations similar to those of its ImageNet-pretrained starting point. It also uses a learning-to-optimize strategy to select layer-specific learning rates automatically. Together, these components aim to balance learning from synthetic data with retaining features that already transfer well to real visual inputs.

The reported experiments show improved synthetic-to-real generalization without training on the target real data, along with benefits for downstream domain adaptation. The role of ImageNet pretraining is essential to interpreting that result: the method preserves previously learned visual knowledge while adapting on synthetic examples. The abstract does not specify which individual representation constraints or learning-rate decisions contribute most to the gains.
icml-2020-automated-synthetic-to-real-ge.tldr: Preserving ImageNet representations and learning layer-specific step sizes improves transfer from synthetic images to real tasks.

paragraphs: Conditional Value-at-Risk summarizes unfavorable outcomes in the tail of a distribution, making estimation accuracy especially sensitive to rare events. This paper asks how quickly estimates become reliable as more samples arrive. It treats sub-Gaussian, light-tailed, and heavy-tailed distributions separately rather than applying one estimator indiscriminately.

For sub-Gaussian and light-tailed variables, the analysis uses the classical empirical-distribution estimator. For heavy-tailed variables, the authors assume a bounded-moment condition and introduce a truncation-based estimator. The resulting concentration bounds decay exponentially with sample size and improve on available bounds for the distribution classes considered.

The paper demonstrates an application to identifying the best arm in a multi-armed bandit according to CVaR under a fixed sampling budget. Its concentration results yield an upper bound on the probability of choosing the wrong arm. The guarantees depend on matching the estimator and its assumptions to the distributional setting, particularly when heavy tails require truncation.
icml-2020-concentration-bounds-for-cvar-.tldr: Distribution-sensitive CVaR estimators obtain tighter concentration bounds and guarantees for risk-based best-arm identification.

paragraphs: An advertisement may contribute to a purchase even when the purchase happens only after several later exposures. Systems that optimize revenue from each exposure independently can miss those delayed contributions. This paper instead studies how to allocate a limited advertising budget across sequences of exposures to maximize cumulative revenue.

The authors formulate sequential advertising as a dynamic knapsack problem. They introduce a bilevel optimization framework with theoretical guarantees that reduces the original solution space while preserving solution quality. An additional action-space reduction method is designed to improve the exploration efficiency of reinforcement learning in this setting.

Offline and online experiments report higher cumulative revenue than the compared state-of-the-art baselines. The work connects a budget-allocation formulation to practical reductions in planning and learning complexity. Its central shift is to value exposures through their contribution to an eventual sequence outcome; the abstract does not provide the numerical revenue gains or the detailed assumptions behind the theoretical guarantees.
icml-2020-dynamic-knapsack-optimization-.tldr: Dynamic knapsack optimization accounts for repeated ad exposures and improves budgeted cumulative revenue in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: In multiple hypothesis testing, analysts often adapt their strategy after seeing promising patterns in the data. That flexibility can invalidate error guarantees built for a procedure chosen in advance. The i-FWER test aims to allow interactive, data-dependent guidance while still controlling the chance of making any false rejection.

The method uses a protocol for masking and unmasking information. A human analyst, or a program acting for the analyst, can guide the testing process adaptively within that protocol. The authors prove familywise error rate control when the protocol is followed, making the permitted information flow part of the statistical guarantee.

Numerical experiments demonstrate the test’s power when genuine signals have structure, and the paper explores additional masking constructions. The contribution is a disciplined way to combine analyst judgment with valid inference. Its flexibility remains conditional on the prescribed interaction rules: the guarantee does not authorize unrestricted inspection and revision of the testing procedure after all information has been revealed.
icml-2020-familywise-error-rate-control-.tldr: Interactive masking lets analysts adapt multiple testing while preserving familywise error control under a specified protocol.

paragraphs: An agent acting under partial observability must choose actions using beliefs about an uncertain state. Sometimes an action is valuable because it reveals information, even if its immediate task reward is small. This paper studies planning with rewards that depend directly on beliefs, including combinations of ordinary reward and expected information gain.

Information Particle Filter Tree, or IPFT, is an online planning algorithm for continuous-domain problems with these belief-dependent rewards. It simulates trajectories of particle-based beliefs and uses Monte Carlo Tree Search to build a search tree in belief space. The approach therefore evaluates how actions change both the task situation and the agent’s uncertainty about it.

The evaluation finds that including information gain substantially improves performance when gathering information is an essential part of an optimal policy. The contribution is a practical planning procedure for that reward formulation, rather than a claim that information gain always improves decision-making. Its usefulness is demonstrated specifically in problems where better-informed beliefs support better subsequent actions.
icml-2020-information-particle-filter-tr.tldr: IPFT plans through particle-based beliefs so continuous-domain agents can explicitly value informative actions.

paragraphs: Contextual language representations had improved many natural-language tasks, but comparable reusable representations and broad evaluation were less established for source code. This paper develops CuBERT and a benchmark to test whether pretrained contextual code embeddings transfer across different program-understanding problems.

The authors curate a deduplicated collection of 7.4 million Python files from GitHub and use it to pretrain a BERT-based code model. They also create an open benchmark containing five classification tasks and one program-repair task. Fine-tuning on this shared collection of tasks makes it possible to evaluate representation quality beyond one narrowly selected use case.

CuBERT outperforms the compared Word2Vec embedding variants, BiLSTM and Transformer models, and published state-of-the-art systems, including settings with shorter training and fewer labeled examples. The released model and benchmark provide reusable resources for subsequent research. The results establish strong performance on the paper’s Python-centered evaluation, without implying equivalent performance across every programming language or software-engineering task.
icml-2020-learning-and-evaluating-contex.tldr: CuBERT pretrains on 7.4 million Python files and improves multiple code-understanding tasks with less labeled data and training.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to infer opinions or states across a social network after observing only a sample of its nodes. The network’s structure supplies information beyond the observed labels themselves. The central question is when those relationships make it possible to learn efficiently from relatively few observations.

The analysis separates two regimes. When the network exhibits strong noise, sample-efficient learning is impossible. When the network is sufficiently stable, the authors provide a polynomial-time learning algorithm. This contrast identifies properties of the network as essential to the feasibility of extrapolating from sampled nodes.

In the stable regime, the algorithm achieves nearly optimal sample complexity. The contribution is therefore both an impossibility result and a constructive guarantee, showing where efficient inference becomes possible. The abstract does not define the precise noise and stability conditions, so those formal definitions are necessary before applying the result to a particular social network or interpreting observed disagreement as evidence of learnability.
icml-2020-learning-opinions-in-social-ne.tldr: Network stability permits nearly sample-optimal opinion learning, while sufficiently strong noise makes efficient learning impossible.
